title: Fix Stale Closure in Interval Callback
concept: Functional State Updates vs Snapshot Closure
problemStatement: In React, `setCount(count + 1)` inside a `setInterval` with an empty dependency array always sees `count = 0`. Implement `createSafeCounter(initialValue)` that uses functional updater semantics `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` so that repeated ticks always compute against the freshest state.
interviewTrap: Writing `state = state + 1` or capturing `state` at closure creation time. Passing an updater function `prev => prev + 1` resolves the current value at invocation time.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Every React render has its own props, state, and event handlers. A closure formed inside an effect or callback captures variables from that specific render snapshot forever unless re-created or accessed via functional updates/useRef.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Why does setInterval inside useEffect capture stale state?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: If `useEffect` has an empty dependency array `[]`, the effect callback runs only once on mount. The interval callback closes over state variables from that initial render pass (e.g. `count = 0`). Every time the interval fires, it reads that stale captured variable. Using functional updates (`setCount(prev => prev + 1)`) or Dan Abramov's `useInterval` with a mutable callback ref solves this.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: The single most famous React Hooks interview trap.

realWorldUseCases.description: Running persistent intervals that access latest state and props without resetting the timer on every keystroke.

howToExplain.opening: Stale closures in timers occur when an asynchronous callback captures a snapshot of state from an older render pass. Functional state updates bypass closure capture by reading from React's pending update queue.
keyPoints: setInterval setup once on mount captures initial render closure.
Adding state to effect dependency array resets the timer on every tick.
Functional updaters (prev => prev + 1) read fresh state without dependencies.
useInterval uses a mutable callback ref to read fresh functions dynamically.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Separating timer duration lifecycle from callback execution prevents timer resetting bugs in React.
analogies: A wall clock with a speaker: instead of recording a message on day 1 that plays forever, the clock calls a live hotline (ref) to ask what to say every minute.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing setCount(count + 1) inside an interval with [] dependencies.
commonMistakes.why: count is captured as 0; 0 + 1 is always 1, so count never increments past 1.

followUpDeepDive.question: How will React 19's useEffectEvent solve this natively?
followUpDeepDive.answer: `useEffectEvent` creates a non-reactive event function that always sees fresh props and state but is omitted from effect dependency arrays, preventing unwanted timer resets.
